name: Quantitative evaluation, version 2
models: Reported, as of Nov 2026: SIG's Quantitative Evaluation. Seventeen questions in 60 minutes with a calculator, rising from quick expected values to multi-stage Bayes and ruin.
description: This is the reported format of SIG's Quantitative Evaluation, as candidates described it by Nov 2026. You have 17 questions in 60 minutes. A calculator is allowed, but the app has none, so have a basic one ready. The questions start with quick expected values and end with multi-stage Bayes and gambler's ruin. Some take a choice, others a number to three decimal places. A wrong answer scores 0, and you may change answers until you submit. Other reports give 16 questions in 20 minutes; this mock follows the longer one. This is version 2 of 3.

items.title: A die that pays squares
items.question: A fair 4-sided die, faces 1 to 4, pays £ the square of the face shown. What is a fair price to play once?

options.why: You squared the average face, $2.5^2$, instead of averaging the squares.
You priced the face itself, not its square.
You added the squares but did not divide by 4.

feedback.correct: The mean of the squares is $\tfrac{15}{2}$, about £7.50.
feedback.generic: Average the squares of the faces, not the square of the average face.

items.title: Cards of one kind
items.question: You deal 13 cards from a well-shuffled 52-card deck. What is the expected number of aces among them?

options.why: You gave the chance for one card, not the count over all 13.
You counted the cards that are not aces.
You used the share of one suit, 1 in 4, instead of one rank, 1 in 13.

feedback.correct: Each card is an ace with chance $\tfrac{1}{13}$, so $13 \times \tfrac{1}{13} = 1$.
feedback.generic: Give each card an indicator for being an ace, then add the chances.

explain.text: Card $j$ is an ace with chance $\tfrac{4}{52} = \tfrac{1}{13}$, whatever the other cards are. Linearity adds the 13 chances: $1$. The cards are dependent, but an expectation does not care.

items.title: A game with a fee
items.question: You pay £3 to roll a fair six-sided die. You receive £ the face if it is 4 or more, and nothing otherwise. What is your expected profit per game?

options.why: You counted only the fee and left out the payout.
You paid out the face on every roll: $3.5 - 3$.
You found the expected payout and forgot the £3 fee.

feedback.correct: The payout averages £2.50, so the profit is −£0.50 a game.
feedback.generic: Average the payout over all six faces, then take off the fee.

explain.text: $E[\text{payout}] = \tfrac{4 + 5 + 6}{6} = 2.5$, so the profit is $2.5 - 3 = -0.5$. Check: half the rolls pay, averaging 5, so $\tfrac12 \times 5 - 3 = -0.5$.

items.title: Pairs of heads
items.question: You toss a fair coin 21 times. Count each place where two heads stand side by side, overlaps included: HHH holds two. What is the expected count?

options.why: You counted 21 places for a pair, but 21 tosses have only 20.
You gave each place chance $\tfrac12$, but both tosses must be heads.
You split the tosses into separate pairs and missed the overlapping ones.

feedback.correct: There are 20 places, each with chance $\tfrac14$: $20 \times \tfrac14 = 5$.
feedback.generic: Give each neighbouring pair of tosses an indicator, then add the chances.

explain.text: Indicator $I_j$ marks heads at tosses $j$ and $j + 1$, for $j = 1$ to $20$. Each has $E[I_j] = \tfrac14$, so the count averages $5$. Overlapping pairs are dependent, but linearity does not care.

items.title: At least one six
items.question: You roll a fair six-sided die 3 times. What is the chance of at least one six? Give three decimal places.

widget.label: Chance of at least one six

feedback.generic: Find the chance of no six at all, then take it from 1.

byKey.times: You added $\tfrac16$ 3 times, which counts rolls with two sixes twice.
byKey.none: That is the chance of no six. Take it from 1.
byKey.one: That is the chance for a single roll.

explain.text: No six in 3 rolls has chance $(\tfrac56)^3 = \tfrac{125}{216}$. So at least one six has chance $\tfrac{91}{216} \approx 0.421$. Check: of the 216 equally likely outcomes, 91 hold a six.

items.title: Two cards, at least one
items.question: You draw two cards from a well-shuffled 52-card deck, without replacement. At least one is a picture card (jack, queen or king). What is the chance that both are picture cards?

options.why: You took the first card as a picture card, but "at least one" could be either card.
You found the chance of two picture cards before using the condition.
You gave the chance that a single card is a picture card.

feedback.correct: 66 pairs of picture cards out of 546 pairs that hold one: $\tfrac{11}{91}$.
feedback.generic: Count unordered pairs: two picture cards, over pairs with at least one.

explain.text: There are $\binom{52}{2} = 1{,}326$ pairs, and $\binom{40}{2} = 780$ hold no picture card. So 546 pairs hold at least one, and $\binom{12}{2} = 66$ hold two. The chance is $\tfrac{66}{546} = \tfrac{11}{91}$.

items.title: Exactly so many heads
items.question: You toss a fair coin 7 times. What is the chance of exactly 2 heads?

options.why: You priced one order, such as HHTTTTT, but there are $\binom{7}{2} = 21$ of them.
You gave the share of heads, $2$ in $7$, as a chance.
You found the chance of at least 2 heads.

feedback.generic: Count the orders with 2 heads, then multiply by the chance of one order.

explain.text: Each sequence of 7 tosses has chance $\tfrac{1}{128}$. Exactly 2 heads happens in $\binom{7}{2} = 21$ of them, so the chance is $\tfrac{21}{128}$.

items.title: The heavy coin
items.question: You have 28 coins that look the same. One is heavier and the rest weigh the same. Using a balance scale, what is the fewest weighings that always finds the heavy coin?

options.why: You split the coins in two each time, which wastes the balanced outcome.
You weighed the coins one pair at a time.
You set one coin against each other coin in turn.

feedback.correct: Each weighing splits the suspects three ways, and $3^{3} < 28 \le 3^{4}$.
feedback.generic: A weighing has three outcomes, so split the coins into three groups.

explain.text: Each weighing has three outcomes: left heavy, right heavy or balanced. So $k$ weighings can single out one coin among at most $3^k$, and $3^{3} = 27 < 28 \le 81$. Put equal groups in the pans and the rest aside, none above 27 coins, then repeat on the suspects.

items.title: A positive test
items.question: A condition affects 1% of people. A test catches 90% of true cases and flags 10% of healthy people by mistake. A person tests positive. What is the chance they have the condition? Give three decimal places.

feedback.generic: Picture 10,000 people and count the true and the false positives.

byKey.hit: That is the chance of a positive given the condition, the wrong way round.
byKey.base: You kept the base rate and ignored the test.

explain.text: In 10,000 people, 100 have it and 90 of them test positive. Of the 9,900 without it, 990 test positive. So $P = \tfrac{90}{90 + 990} = \tfrac{1}{12} \approx 0.083$.

items.title: Waiting for a pattern
items.question: You toss a fair coin until HTH first appears in consecutive tosses. What is the expected number of tosses?

options.why: You took one over the chance of HTH, which is the gap between repeats, not the first wait.
You waited for HT, 4 tosses, and assumed the next toss obliges.
You counted every prefix as an overlap, as for HHH, but HT does not end in H.

feedback.correct: Solving the state equations gives 10 tosses.
feedback.generic: Write one equation per state of progress, from scratch to one short of the pattern.

explain.text: From scratch a tail changes nothing, so $E_0 = 2 + E_H$; from H a head keeps H, so $E_H = 2 + E_{HT}$. From HT a head ends it and a tail restarts: $E_{HT} = 1 + \tfrac12 E_0$. So $E_0 = 5 + \tfrac12 E_0$, giving $E_0 = 10$.

items.title: Roll again or keep
items.question: A fair 6-sided die, faces 1 to 6, pays £ the face. After the first roll you may reroll up to twice, and you must keep the last face rolled. Under the best rule, what is the game worth?

options.why: You never rerolled, so you took the plain average.
You valued the game with one reroll, not two.
You took the largest face rolled, but a reroll throws the old face away.

feedback.correct: Keep 5 or 6 first, as the rest of the game is worth £4.25.
feedback.generic: Work backwards: keep a face only if it beats the value of rolling again.

explain.text: With one reroll left the game is worth £4.25, as the last roll is worth £3.50. So on the first roll keep only a face above 4.25: 5 or 6. The value is $\tfrac{5 + 6}{6} + \tfrac{4}{6} \times 4.25 = \tfrac{14}{3}$, about £4.67.

items.title: One face of two dice
items.question: You roll two fair 6-sided dice, faces 1 to 6. What is the expected value of the smaller face? If they tie, that face counts. Give three decimal places.

feedback.generic: Find $P(\min \ge k)$ first: both dice must be at least $k$.

byKey.one: That is the mean of one die; the smaller of two is pulled down.
byKey.other: That is the expected larger face.
byKey.distinct: You left out the doubles, which are as likely as any other ordered pair.

explain.text: Both dice must be at least $k$, so $P(\min \ge k) = (\tfrac{7 - k}{6})^2$. Then $E[\min] = \sum_k P(\min \ge k) = \tfrac{36 + 25 + 16 + \dots + 1}{36} = \tfrac{91}{36} \approx 2.528$. Check: $E[\max] + E[\min] = 7$, and $E[\max] = \tfrac{161}{36}$.

items.title: The two-headed coin
items.question: A bag holds 3 fair coins and one coin with two heads. You draw a coin at random and toss it 4 times. It shows 4 heads. What is the chance it is the two-headed coin?

options.why: You kept the prior $\tfrac{1}{4}$ and ignored the 4 heads.
You gave the two kinds of coin equal priors, but fair coins outnumber it 3 to 1.
You found the chance of 4 heads, not the chance of the coin.

feedback.generic: Weigh each kind of coin by its prior times its chance of 4 heads.

explain.text: Prior odds are $1 : 3$, and 4 heads are $2^4 = 16$ times likelier with the two-headed coin. Posterior odds are $16 : 3$, so $P = \tfrac{16}{19}$. Check: $\tfrac{1/4}{1/4 + 3/4 \times 1/16} = \tfrac{16}{19}$.

items.title: Two positive tests
items.question: A condition affects 1% of people. A test catches 90% of true cases and flags 10% of healthy people. One person takes it twice, with independent results, and is positive both times. What is the chance they have the condition? Give three decimal places.

feedback.generic: Each positive multiplies the odds by $\tfrac{90}{10}$.

byKey.once: That uses one positive only. Update the odds again for the second.
byKey.square: You squared the hit rate and ignored the false positives.

explain.text: Prior odds are $\tfrac{1}{99}$, and each positive multiplies them by $\tfrac{90}{10} = 9$. Two positives give odds $\tfrac{9}{11}$, so $P = \tfrac{9}{20} \approx 0.450$. Check: $\tfrac{0.01 \times 0.9^2}{0.01 \times 0.9^2 + 0.99 \times 0.1^2}$ gives the same.

items.title: How long a fair game lasts
items.question: You start with £2 and bet £1 at a time on a fair coin. You stop when you reach £0 or £8. What is the expected number of bets?

options.why: You counted the steps to £8 as if every bet were a win.
You multiplied 2 by 8; the formula uses the distances to both ends.
You squared the distance to £8 and ignored the floor at £0.

explain.text: The duration $D_k$ satisfies $D_k = 1 + \tfrac12(D_{k-1} + D_{k+1})$, with $D_0 = D_{8} = 0$. Its solution is $D_k = k(8 - k)$, so $D_2 = 12$. Check: $1 + \tfrac12(D_1 + D_3) = 1 + \tfrac12(7 + 15) = 12$.

items.title: Ruin with an edge
items.question: You start with £3. Each £1 bet wins with chance 0.55, independently. You stop when you reach £0 or £6. What is the chance you reach £6? Give three decimal places.

feedback.generic: Use $P_i = \tfrac{1 - r^i}{1 - r^N}$, where $r = \tfrac{q}{p}$ is the losing odds.

byKey.fair: That is the fair-coin answer $\tfrac{3}{6}$, but the edge is on your side.
byKey.streak: You needed 3 wins in a row, but losses can be won back.
byKey.one: That is the chance of winning a single bet.

explain.text: $P_k$ solves $P_k = pP_{k+1} + qP_{k-1}$ with $P_0 = 0$ and $P_{6} = 1$, so $P_k = \tfrac{1 - r^k}{1 - r^{6}}$ with $r = \tfrac{q}{p} = \tfrac{9}{11}$. So $P_3 = \tfrac{1 - (9/11)^3}{1 - (9/11)^{6}} = \tfrac{1331}{2060} \approx 0.646$. Check: shooting $P_{k+1} = (P_k - qP_{k-1})/p$ from $P_0 = 0$ gives the same.

items.title: Which coin got you there
items.question: A coin is either fair or lands heads with chance two in three, each equally likely. You start with £1 and bet £1 on heads at each toss. You stop at £0 or £3. You reach £3. What is the chance the coin is the biased one? Give three decimal places.

feedback.generic: Find each coin's chance of reaching £3, then use Bayes with equal priors.

byKey.stage: That is the chance of reaching £3. Now condition on having reached it.
byKey.biased: That is the biased coin's chance of reaching £3, not the posterior.
byKey.prior: You kept the prior and ignored that you reached £3.

explain.text: From £1 a fair coin reaches £3 with chance $\tfrac13$, and the biased one with $\tfrac{1 - r}{1 - r^3} = \tfrac{4}{7}$, where $r = \tfrac{1}{2}$. The equal priors cancel, so $P = \tfrac{4/7}{1/3 + 4/7} = \tfrac{12}{19} \approx 0.632$.
